claims.text: Coupling HTXRD, real-time TGA, and optical spectroscopy can simultaneously monitor high-temperature oxidation kinetics and phase transformations.
The integrated method can decouple overlapping oxidation and phase-transformation events.
The proposed specimen is a homogenized advanced alloy or coating, such as a high-entropy alloy, with a characterized initial phase structure.
The material is exposed to a controlled high-temperature oxidizing environment during integrated in situ measurement.
High-temperature oxidation can involve rapid and overlapping oxidation and phase-transformation events.
High-temperature oxidation causes oxide-phase formation and time-dependent phase transformations.
Oxide formation and phase transformations alter the material's crystalline structure.
Oxide formation and phase transformations can be detected through distinct diffraction peaks and mass changes.
HTXRD captures real-time, time-temperature-dependent phase evolution during high-temperature oxidation.
TGA measures oxidation through sample mass gain.
Optical spectroscopy provides chemical-state information during oxidation.
Combining temporal and spectral information from HTXRD, TGA, and optical spectroscopy permits separation of overlapping oxidation and phase-transformation events.
The integrated method will produce distinct time-resolved signatures of oxidation kinetics, including mass gain and oxide formation.
The integrated method will produce distinct time-resolved signatures of phase transformations through changes in diffraction patterns and optical spectra.
Oxidation and phase-transformation signatures cannot be separated using HTXRD alone.
Conventional in situ HTXRD has difficulty distinguishing signals from rapid, overlapping oxidation and phase changes.
The temporal resolution of TGA and optical spectroscopy may be insufficient for very fast oxidation kinetics.
TGA and optical spectroscopy may be unable to distinguish subtle phase changes, leaving partial signal overlap.
It is uncertain whether the temporal resolution of all three techniques is sufficient to completely decouple rapid, overlapping events.
A failure of the integrated measurements to provide additional separation relative to an HTXRD-only control would falsify the hypothesis.
